passage:
Monday: Sunaina wrote “study more” at the top of her planner and sat there for forty minutes with the maths book closed. She wasn't sure what “more” meant, so she scrolled her phone and felt worse.

Wednesday: Her deskmate Arnab showed her his planner, where one line read, “Ch. 3, page 41, sums 1 to 5.” Sunaina copied the style. She solved the five sums in twenty minutes.

Saturday: she wrote “Ch. 3, sums 6 to 10, then check answers” and had a tick beside it before lunch. Study felt like something with edges now.

qa.q: What line did Arnab have in his planner?
qa.a: Arnab's line read, “Ch. 3, page 41, sums 1 to 5.”

qa.q: Why did Sunaina scroll her phone on Monday?
qa.a: Sunaina did not know what “more” meant, so she felt stuck and uneasy, and scrolling was easier than sitting with that feeling.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday to help Sunaina start?
qa.a: She replaced a vague goal with a first physical action, chapter three, page 41, five sums, which gave her something to grip. 😊

qa.q: What might Arnab think when Sunaina copies his planner style?
qa.a: Arnab may feel pleased and a little proud that a simple habit of his was useful to Sunaina.

grounding: A teenager writes a vague study goal, sits without a start, then a concrete first action makes beginning possible.

passage: “You keep a stub of pencil and a torn card in your shirt pocket, Abhinav, and you asked why. Come, sit. I'm Gautam, and when I was fifteen, I wrote 'study hard' on the calendar above my bed and felt very noble about it. For a week I sat at the desk every evening, opened the book, looked at the ceiling and got up again. I didn't know where to put my hands. My cousin saw me and said, 'What will you do in the first ten minutes?' I said I didn't know. So I wrote: 'Algebra, exercise 4, questions 1 to 5.' Five questions. I could see the end of them. That night the pencil moved, and the ceiling stopped mattering.”

qa.q: What did the narrator write on the calendar at fifteen?
qa.a: At fifteen, Gautam wrote “study hard” on the calendar above the bed.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel at the desk during that week?
qa.a: Gautam felt lost and stuck: opening the book, looking at the ceiling and giving up showed there was nothing concrete to hold on to.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gautam begin?
qa.a: Gautam's cousin asked what Gautam would do in the first ten minutes, and Gautam answered by writing exercise 4, questions 1 to 5.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt asking that question?
qa.a: The cousin was probably concerned and curious, wanting to help without giving the answer, and simply asked what came first.

grounding: A teenager's vague goal leaves the mind with nothing to grip until a concrete first step is written.

passage:
Arohi: "Done! Study plan for the week."
Darshan: "Show me."
Arohi: "Monday, study. Tuesday, study. Wednesday, study."
Darshan: "Study what?"
Arohi: "Maths. Everything. I'll figure it out."
Darshan: "Remember last week? You sat with your book open for an hour and texted me memes."
Arohi: "That's because I didn't know where to start."
Darshan: "So start with something your hands can do. Like, chapter three, sums one to five."
Arohi: "That's so small."
Darshan: "Small is good. You'll actually do it."
Arohi: "Fine. Monday: chapter three, sums one to five. Tuesday: six to ten."
Darshan: "Now it's a plan 👍"
Arohi: "Ugh. You're right."

qa.q: What did Arohi's first plan say for Monday?
qa.a: The first plan said "Monday, study."

qa.q: How did Arohi feel sitting with the book open last week?
qa.a: Arohi felt lost and stuck, not knowing where to start, so the memes were an escape.

qa.q: What would you advise Arohi to keep doing?
qa.a: Write each day's plan as a specific action, like a numbered set of sums from one chapter, so the starting point is obvious.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Arohi's first plan?
qa.a: Darshan sees it as too vague to act on, and gently teases Arohi into making it concrete.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teenager whose vague study plan leaves no place to start until it becomes a concrete first action.

passage: I'm Jomon, and in Class Nine I wrote "Study physics" on a sticky note and put it above my desk. Every evening I sat down, looked at it and felt blank. Study what? Which chapter? I'd flip pages and end up drawing in the margins. My brother Gautam, who was in college, saw the note and laughed. "That's not a plan, that's a wish." He took the note and wrote: "Read page 45. Solve question 2." I did it in twenty minutes. The next day I wrote my own: "Solve questions 3 and 4." Small, but I finally knew where to put my pencil.

qa.q: What did Jomon write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Jomon wrote "Study physics" on a sticky note.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel looking at the note each evening?
qa.a: Jomon felt blank and lost, unsure which chapter or task to start with.

qa.q: What changed that helped Jomon start?
qa.a: Gautam replaced the vague note with a physical action, read page 45 and solve question 2, which Jomon could finish in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Gautam see the note at first?
qa.a: Gautam sees it as a wish, not a plan, since it gives no first step; he laughs, but then helps.

grounding: A teenager looks back on a vague study goal that gave no starting point until it became a concrete first action.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Sunaina, Class 10, came to see me after a mock exam. She said she had "studied every day" but felt she had got nowhere. I asked her to show me her plan. Every line read "Study maths" or "Revise science". When I asked where she began each evening, she said she usually opened the book and scrolled her phone. We rewrote Monday together: "Solve five sums from chapter 3, exercise 3.2." Her friend Sarika joined us and did the same for chemistry. I will check in with Sunaina next Thursday to see if the specific steps helped.

qa.q: What did every line of Sunaina's plan read?
qa.a: Every line read "Study maths" or "Revise science".

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after the mock exam?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and discouraged, because she had studied every day but felt she had got nowhere.

qa.q: How did the counsellor support Sunaina?
qa.a: The counsellor asked where she began each evening and rewrote Monday's plan as five specific sums from exercise 3.2.

qa.q: How might Sarika be affected by joining the session?
qa.a: Sarika could benefit too, turning her own vague chemistry plan into a clear first step alongside her friend.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager whose vague study goal gives no starting point until it becomes a concrete task.

passage:
Tuesday night.
My plan for tonight said "Revise history." That's it. I sat at the desk at seven with the textbook, the notebook and my water bottle, and I just… sat. Where do you even start with "history"? The whole book? The Mughals? The maps?
By eight I had sharpened three pencils and rearranged my shelf.
Ramesh bhaiya came in to borrow the charger and saw my face. "What are you revising?"
"History."
"What's the first thing your hand will actually do?"
I didn't know what he meant. He said, "Not 'revise.' Like, 'read pages 40 to 44 and write five dates on a card.'"
So I wrote exactly that. And I did it, in twenty-five minutes. Then I wrote the next one: "Label the six places on the map on page 46." Did that too.
I'm Madhuri, and I've been writing "study more" for two years. Tomorrow's plan will have a page number in it.

qa.q: Which pages did Ramesh bhaiya suggest reading?
qa.a: Pages 40 to 44.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel sitting at the desk from seven to eight?
qa.a: Madhuri felt stuck and lost, not knowing where to start, so pencils got sharpened instead.

qa.q: What made Madhuri's second plan work?
qa.a: It named a physical first action with page numbers and a small output, like writing five dates on a card, which gave the mind something to grip.

qa.q: How might Ramesh bhaiya feel if he saw tomorrow's plan?
qa.a: Ramesh bhaiya would probably feel pleased and a bit proud that his small tip changed how Madhuri plans.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose vague goal of revising history leaves her stuck, until a concrete first step with page numbers gets her moving.
